headline: Power outages, heavy rain continue on East Coast after Thanksgiving Day storm
author: Victoria Craw

paragraphs.text: More than 700,000 people remained without power mainly across the East Coast early Friday after the worst Thanksgiving Day storm in decades battered the region, flooding coastal communities and disrupting travel.

The storm “continues to bring widespread inclement weather this morning for a large portion of the eastern U.S.,” the National Weather Service said, adding that there was wet snow “as far south as the Tennessee Valley,” and “freezing rain” across northern New England, on Friday morning.
Power outages were recorded in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, Missouri and New York.

The storm has affected tens of millions of people across the East Coast from North Carolina to New York, with ocean tides hitting record levels in some places, bridges closed, trees uprooted and infrastructure damaged by wind and waves.
Shorelines in Washington, D.C., and Baltimore remained under a coastal flood warning early Friday linked to high tides, with water levels expected to be up to three feet above normal in some places.

New York City also remained under a coastal flood warning early Friday, after being battered by high winds and rain. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said two people had to be rescued from their cars in the extreme weather. The storm forced the postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday, the first time in the event’s 100-year history it was postponed due to weather.

On Friday, conditions are expected to improve across the East Coast as the storm begins to weaken, though the vast size of the system means it will take some time to dissipate, the National Weather Service said.
The storm brought up to 15 inches of snow in eastern Missouri, according to the NWS.

Huge waves and storm surges flooded streets in North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey and New York, officials reported. Several communities reported record high water levels, including a six-foot rise in Wachapreague, Virginia, which broke a 1998 record by more than 2.1 feet.
The NWS has reminded people to never drive through flooded roadways, and warned of significant coastal flooding and beach erosion along the Mid-Atlantic and New England coasts.
